title: Methamphetamine and amphetamines
why_this_matters: Stimulant exposure is a duty hazard for working dogs. Street drugs are often adulterated, so presentations are non-specific, and most dogs improve with prompt treatment but severe cases can die [1][4].

what_changes_from_human.point: Presentations are non-specific because illicit drugs are adulterated with other substances [1].
Rapid on-site drug tests give many false positives because of low specificity [1].

recognition: A methamphetamine case report (one 3.7 kg dog): extreme agitation, seizures, tachycardia, hyperthermia, hypertension, dilated pupils and disseminated intravascular coagulation [3].
In a lisdexamfetamine case, early neurological signs progressed to severe respiratory and cardiovascular signs and cardiopulmonary arrest, with widespread hemorrhage at necropsy [4].
One dog with amphetamine toxicosis developed severe rhabdomyolysis with myoglobinuria and recovered without kidney injury [5].
management: With prompt treatment the prognosis of amphetamine toxicosis in dogs is generally considered good, but a fatal case shows that prompt treatment does not always prevent death [4].

Intravenous lipid emulsion in 313 poisoned dogs (mostly mixed or unidentified toxicants, not stimulants specifically) had a positive effect in 74%, worsened signs in 4% and had suspected adverse effects in 6%; overall survival was 96%. The authors advise careful individual selection [6].
In one amphetamine case, serum amphetamine concentrations were lower 1 hour after lipid emulsion, which was the only treatment given in that hour (single case) [2].

TODO: a canine stimulant treatment protocol (sedation, cooling, seizure and blood pressure control) from the Oster 2023 full text or the veterinary reviewer. Only case reports were retrieved for methamphetamine.

takeaway: Treat an agitated, hyperthermic, tachycardic dog as a possible stimulant exposure, do not trust a rapid drug test, and get the dog to a veterinarian.
